claim: The zona incerta is a subthalamic nucleus made up mostly of GABAergic neurons.
source: The zona incerta is a subthalamic nucleus made up mostly of GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the composition of the zona incerta.

claim: The zona incerta has wide-ranging inputs and outputs.
source: It has wide-ranging inputs and outputs and is believed to have many integrative functions that link sensory stimuli with motor responses to guide behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature in the introduction.

claim: The zona incerta is believed to have many integrative functions that link sensory stimuli with motor responses to guide behavior.
source: It has wide-ranging inputs and outputs and is believed to have many integrative functions that link sensory stimuli with motor responses to guide behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about existing beliefs in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Two groups of zona incerta neurons exist based on their sensitivity to movement.
source: We found two groups of neurons based on their sensitivity to movement, with a minority of neurons responding to whisker stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 1.

claim: A minority of zona incerta neurons respond to whisker stimuli.
source: We found two groups of neurons based on their sensitivity to movement, with a minority of neurons responding to whisker stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 showing that 19.4% of neurons responded to whisker stimulation.

claim: Zona incerta GABAergic neurons robustly code the occurrence of exploratory and goal-directed movements.
source: Furthermore, zona incerta GABAergic neurons robustly code the occurrence of exploratory and goal-directed movements, but not their direction.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data in Figures 3-7.

claim: Zona incerta GABAergic neurons do not code the direction of movement.
source: Furthermore, zona incerta GABAergic neurons robustly code the occurrence of exploratory and goal-directed movements, but not their direction.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing similar activation for ipsiversive and contraversive movements.

claim: The zona incerta has a role in modulating the movement associated with exploratory and goal-directed behaviors.
source: The results showed that the zona incerta has a role in modulating the movement associated with these behaviors, but this has little impact on overall performance.
evidence: This is supported by lesion and optogenetic manipulation data in Figures 8-11.

claim: Zona incerta modulation of movement has little impact on overall behavioral performance.
source: The results showed that the zona incerta has a role in modulating the movement associated with these behaviors, but this has little impact on overall performance.
evidence: This is supported by lesion data in Figure 8 showing minimal effects on avoidance performance.

claim: Zona incerta neurons distribute a broad corollary signal of movement occurrence to their diverse projection sites.
source: Zona incerta neurons distribute a broad corollary signal of movement occurrence to their diverse projection sites, which regulates behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data showing movement-related activation and projection-specific effects.

claim: The zona incerta has been associated with regulating thalamocortical and thalamostriatal transmission through its GABAergic projections to the posterior thalamus.
source: The zona incerta has been associated with a variety of functions, including regulating thalamocortical and thalamostriatal transmission through its GABAergic projections to the posterior thalamus (Trageser and Keller, 2004; Lavallée et al., 2005; Trageser et al., 2006; Urbain and Deschênes, 2007; Watson et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The zona incerta contributes to binge eating through its projections to the paraventricular thalamus.
source: contributing to binge eating through its projections to the paraventricular thalamus (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta promotes feeding through projections to the ventral tegmental area.
source: and promoting feeding through projections to the ventral tegmental area (de Git et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta has been implicated in defensive behaviors through its projections to the periaqueductal gray.
source: The zona incerta has also been implicated in defensive behaviors through its projections to the periaqueductal gray (Chou et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta regulates cross-modality enhancement of flight through its projections to the posterior medial nucleus of thalamus.
source: regulating cross-modality enhancement of flight through its projections to the posterior medial nucleus of thalamus (Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta promotes sleep through subsets of its GABAergic neurons.
source: and promoting sleep through subsets of its GABAergic neurons (Liu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta has been linked to mediating Pavlovian fear conditioning and anxiety.
source: In addition, the zona incerta has been linked to other behaviors, such as mediating Pavlovian fear conditioning and anxiety (Li et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2018; Venkataraman et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta controls predatory hunting.
source: controlling predatory hunting (Zhao et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta is involved in novelty seeking.
source: novelty seeking (Ogasawara et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta is involved in itch.
source: itch (Li et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta is involved in neuropathic pain.
source: and neuropathic pain (Masri et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta has been suggested as a site to alleviate essential tremor with deep brain stimulation.
source: It has also been suggested as a site to alleviate essential tremor with deep brain stimulation (Plaha et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The zona incerta has been implicated in motor control.
source: and implicated in motor control (Mitrofanis, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Projections from the zona incerta to the midbrain tegmentum can control learned, cued avoidance locomotor movement.
source: Furthermore, projections from the zona incerta to the midbrain tegmentum can control learned, cued avoidance locomotor movement, but this function is not essential for driving the behavior (Hormigo et al., 2019; Hormigo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Zona incerta control of learned, cued avoidance locomotor movement is not essential for driving the behavior.
source: Furthermore, projections from the zona incerta to the midbrain tegmentum can control learned, cued avoidance locomotor movement, but this function is not essential for driving the behavior (Hormigo et al., 2019; Hormigo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Zona incerta has been proposed to have broad integrative functions.
source: Zona incerta has been proposed to have broad integrative functions (Mitrofanis, 2005; Wang et al., 2020a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Zona incerta has been proposed to serve as an inhibitory switchboard for behavioral control.
source: including serving as an inhibitory switchboard for behavioral control (Fratzl and Hofer, 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Internal copies of motor commands, called corollary discharges or efference copy signals, can affect other brain processes, such as sensory processing.
source: In the brain, internal copies of motor commands, called corollary discharges or efference copy signals, can affect other brain processes, such as sensory processing (Grüsser, 1995; Sommer and Wurtz, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Corollary discharge signals have a critical regulatory role in brain function but are typically not required to generate the behaviors they monitor or signal.
source: These signals have a critical regulatory role in brain function but are typically not required to generate the behaviors they monitor or signal.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge regarding corollary discharge signals.

claim: 341 units were recorded in the zona incerta area.
source: As mice moved on the treadmill, we recorded units in the zona incerta area (n = 341).
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of units recorded.

claim: PCA classification revealed two major groups of zona incerta neurons (Class1 and Class2) that had different coding of movement.
source: This revealed two major groups of neurons (Class1 and Class2) that had different coding of movement and could each be further subclassified into two subgroups (a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Class1 neurons activated robustly during movement.
source: Class1 neurons activated robustly during movement (Figure 1C, D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Class1a neurons (n = 23, 6.7%) had higher firing rates than Class1b neurons (n = 82, 24.1%).
source: Class1a (n = 23, 6.7%) neurons had higher firing rates than Class1b (n = 82, 24.1%) neurons (Tukey q = 12.36, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the firing rate data.

claim: Class2a neurons were somewhat inhibited during movement (n = 80, 23.5%).
source: Class2a were somewhat inhibited during movement (n = 80, 23.5%)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Class2b neurons were weakly activated during movement (n = 156, 45.7%).
source: and Class2b were weakly activated during movement (n = 156, 45.7%).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Class2a neurons had higher firing rates than Class2b neurons.
source: In addition, Class2a neurons had higher firing rates than Class2b neurons (Tukey q = 9.48, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the firing rate data.

claim: Class2a neurons had firing rates equivalent to Class1b neurons.
source: but equivalent to Class1b neurons (Tukey q = 0.54, p = 0.9814).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the firing rate data.

claim: Class1a and Class1b neurons had equivalent positive correlations between speed and firing.
source: Moreover, Class1a and Class1b neurons had equivalent positive correlations between speed and firing (Tukey q = 0.07, p = 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: Class2a neurons had weaker positive correlations than all the other subgroups, including Class2b neurons.
source: Because Class2a neurons could suppress their firing during movement they had weaker positive correlations than all the other subgroups, including Class2b neurons (Tukey q = 4.42, p = 0.01)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: Class1b neurons had higher correlations than Class2b neurons.
source: Class1b neurons had higher correlations than Class2b neurons (Tukey q = 4.54, p = 0.0079).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: There was no difference in recording depth between the four classes of neurons.
source: There was no difference in recording depth between the four classes of neurons (analysis of variance [ANOVA] F(3,337) = 1.06, p = 0.3676).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of recording depth data.

claim: The tested units (n = 170) did not respond to the auditory tone, white noise, or to single air-puffs applied to the lower back.
source: The tested units (n = 170) did not respond to the auditory tone, white noise, or to single air-puffs applied to the lower back (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A portion of the neurons (n = 33, 19.4%) responded to air-puffs aimed at the contralateral whiskers.
source: However, a portion of the neurons (n = 33, 19.4%) responded to air-puffs aimed at the contralateral whiskers (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Units with the strongest contralateral whisker-evoked responses also responded to the ipsilateral whiskers with weaker responses.
source: The units with the strongest contralateral whisker-evoked responses also responded to the ipsilateral whiskers with weaker responses (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Whisker-sensitive neurons did not fall into a specific class of movement-sensitive neurons.
source: Whisker-sensitive neurons did not fall into a specific class of movement-sensitive neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: About half of whisker-sensitive units belonged to Class1 (n = 15/33).
source: About half of these units belonged to Class1 (n = 15/33) indicating that they activated during movement (Figure 2B, black).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The other whisker-sensitive units (n = 18/33) were poorly modulated by movement.
source: The other whisker-sensitive units (n = 18/33) were poorly modulated by movement (Figure 2B, red).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The effect of sensory stimuli on zona incerta neurons depended on the whisker sensitivity of the cells.
source: The effect of the sensory stimuli depended on the whisker sensitivity of the cells (mixed ANOVA interaction of Stimulus × Whisker sensitivity F(3,555) = 156.81, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the sensory response data.

claim: Only whisker-sensitive cells showed a stronger response to contralateral whisker stimulation compared to other stimuli including ipsilateral whiskers.
source: Thus, only the whisker-sensitive cells showed a stronger response to the contralateral (Tukey's t(555) = 24, p < 0.0001 vs the other stimuli including ipsilateral whiskers) or ipsilateral (Tukey's t(555) = 5, p < 0.009 vs the auditory stimuli) whisker stimulation compared to the other stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the sensory response data.

claim: For whisker-sensitive cells, there was no interaction between whisker stimulation side and class.
source: For whisker-sensitive cells (Figure 2D), there was no interaction between whisker stimulation side and class (mixed ANOVA interaction F(1,43) = 1.92, p = 0.17)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Within each class of whisker-sensitive neurons, contralateral whisker stimulation produced stronger responses than ipsilateral stimulation.
source: Although within each class, contralateral whisker stimulation produced stronger responses than ipsilateral stimulation (Tukey t(43) = 8.0, p < 0.0001 for Class1 and Tukey t(43) = 5.6, p = 0.001 for Class2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the whisker response data.

claim: For whisker-sensitive neurons, spontaneous firing rate differed per class.
source: Finally, for whisker-sensitive neurons, spontaneous firing rate differed per class (Figure 2E; two-sample t-test t(43) = 3.7, p = 0.0006).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate data.

claim: Overall movement, including both rotational and translational components, were strongly correlated with zona incerta GABAergic neuron activation.
source: Overall movement, including both rotational and translational components, were strongly correlated with zona incerta GABAergic neuron activation.
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a strong linear positive correlation between movement and zona incerta F/Fo.
source: We also calculated the linear fit between the movement and F/Fo by integrating over a 200-ms window, which revealed a strong linear positive correlation (Figure 3B, lower).
evidence: This is supported by linear fit analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relation between movement and zona incerta activation was absent when one of the variables in the pair was shuffled.
source: This relation was absent when one of the variables in the pair was shuffled (Figure 3B, lower).
evidence: This is supported by shuffled control analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All categories of detected movements were associated with significant zona incerta activation compared to baseline activity.
source: For the three categories of movement peaks, the zona incerta activation around movement was significant compared to baseline activity (Tukey p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the movement-related activation data.

claim: Zona incerta neurons discharge in relation to the occurrence of movement.
source: Thus, zona incerta neurons discharge in relation to the occurrence of movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the movement detection analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the amplitude, area, or timing of the F/Fo activation between contraversive and ipsiversive head movements.
source: There was no significant difference in the amplitude, area, or timing of the F/Fo activation (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Zona incerta neurons do not code the orienting direction of head movements.
source: indicating that zona incerta neurons do not code the orienting direction of head movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the directional movement analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Zona incerta GABAergic neurons discharge in relation to ongoing movement in either direction providing a generalized movement signal to the distributed network of sites where they project.
source: Instead, zona incerta GABAergic neurons discharge in relation to ongoing movement in either direction providing a generalized movement signal to the distributed network of sites where they project.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the directional movement analysis.

claim: The activation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons in relation to movement direction contrasts with the activation of neurons in the superior colliculus.
source: The activation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons in relation to movement direction contrasts with the activation of neurons in other brain areas; for example, superior colliculus neurons measured with the same methods discriminate movement direction (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work cited.

claim: The calcium signal evoked in zona incerta neurons by auditory tones depended on SPL and frequency.
source: The calcium signal evoked in zona incerta neurons by the tones (0–1.5 s window) depended on SPL (TwoWayRMAnova F(1,36) = 92.21, p < 0.0001) and frequency (F(4,144) = 22.18, p < 0.0001), but not their interaction (F(4,144) = 1.8, p = 0.13).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of auditory mapping data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Higher SPL and frequency tones produced stronger zona incerta activation.
source: In general, higher SPL and frequency tones produced stronger zona incerta activation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The movement evoked by auditory tones also depended on tone SPL and frequency.
source: Thus, the movement evoked by the tones also depended on tone SPL (F(1,36) = 89, p < 0.0001) and frequency (F(4,144) = 16.66, p < 0.0001), but not their interaction (F(4,144) = 0.62, p = 0.65).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Zona incerta GABAergic neurons respond robustly to salient auditory tones in association with movement.
source: The results indicate that zona incerta GABAergic neurons respond robustly to salient auditory tones in association with movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the auditory mapping data.

claim: Isoflurane anesthesia led to a reversible strong suppression or abolishment of zona incerta activation evoked by tones.
source: This led to a reversible strong suppression or abolishment of zona incerta activation evoked by the tones (Tukey t(8) = 4.3, p < 0.008, Head Fixed vs +Isoflurane; 0–2 s area)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Isoflurane anesthesia led to a reversible strong suppression or abolishment of zona incerta activation evoked by white noise.
source: white noise (Tukey t(8) = 12.5, p < 0.0001, Head Fixed vs +Isoflurane)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Isoflurane anesthesia led to a reversible strong suppression or abolishment of zona incerta activation evoked by whisker stimuli.
source: and whisker stimuli (Tukey t(8) = 8.07, p = 0.001, Head Fixed vs +Isoflurane).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Activation of zona incerta neurons by sensory stimulation is primarily associated with states when sensory-evoked movement is also present.
source: the results indicate that activation of zona incerta neurons by sensory stimulation is primarily associated with states when sensory-evoked movement is also present.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anesthesia experiment data.

claim: During AA1, the CS caused a very small but noticeable F/Fo peak at CS onset that is associated with a typical orienting head movement.
source: During AA1, the CS caused a very small but noticeable F/Fo peak at CS onset (Figure 6C) that is associated with a typical orienting head movement that occurs at CS onset depending on task contingencies and SPL (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the absence of orienting movement, the tone did not evoke a noticeable activation of zona incerta neurons at CS onset.
source: In the absence of orienting movement, the tone did not evoke a noticeable activation of zona incerta neurons at CS onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The avoidance movement was associated with strong zona incerta neuron activation.
source: While CS onset produced little activation, the succeeding avoidance movement was associated with strong zona incerta neuron activation (Figure 6C avoids from CS onset; note that since avoids occur at different latencies after CS onset they are best measured from their occurrence as in Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: In AA1, there was a large F/Fo peak that followed the avoidance movement.
source: In AA1, there was a large F/Fo peak that followed the avoidance movement.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: As mice transitioned to AA2, the zona incerta activation shifted to the right following the delayed avoidance latencies characteristic of this procedure.
source: As mice transitioned to AA2, the zona incerta activation shifted to the right following the delayed avoidance latencies characteristic of this procedure (Figure 6C, black vs red traces).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The activation of zona incerta neurons is closely associated with the active avoidance movement.
source: Thus, the activation of zona incerta neurons is closely associated with the active avoidance movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the avoidance task data.

claim: When mice failed to avoid, zona incerta neurons activated very sharply in association with the fast escape responses evoked by the US during the escape interval.
source: In addition, when mice failed to avoid, zona incerta neurons activated very sharply in association with the fast escape responses evoked by the US during the escape interval (Figure 6C, escapes).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: During the AA3 procedure, only CS1, which drives active avoidance responses, produced strong zona incerta activation.
source: Furthermore, during the AA3 procedure, only CS1, which drives active avoidance responses, produced strong zona incerta activation (Figure 6C, green).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CS2, which drives passive avoidance, produced nil activation and movement.
source: CS2, which drives passive avoidance, produced nil activation and movement (Figure 6C, blue).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both avoids and escapes were associated with robust zona incerta activation during the three procedures.
source: Both avoids and escapes were associated with robust zona incerta activation during the three procedures (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Escapes were faster and produced stronger activation than avoids for AA1, AA2, and AA3.
source: Moreover, escapes were faster (Tukey t(7) = 7.53, p = 0.0011) and produced stronger activation than avoids (Tukey t(7) = 5.44, p = 0.0063) for AA1, AA2, and AA3.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: During AA4, mice adapt their avoidance movement to the duration of the avoidance interval signaled by each of the three CSs.
source: During AA4, mice adapt their avoidance movement to the duration of the avoidance interval signaled by each of the three CSs (Hormigo et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Zona incerta activation shifted to reflect the avoidance movement during AA4.
source: Accordingly, zona incerta activation shifted to reflect the avoidance movement (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CS1 avoids were faster than CS2 or CS3 avoids during AA4.
source: the CS1 avoids were faster than CS2 (Tukey t(10) = 6.78, p = 0.0019) or CS3 avoids (Tukey t(10) = 5.86, p = 0.0051)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There was no difference in the peak activation of zona incerta neurons between CS1, CS2, and CS3 during AA4.
source: However, this was not reflected in a difference of the peak activation of zona incerta neurons (RMAnova F(2,10) = 0.09, p = 0.91)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Zona incerta activation was closely associated with movement during the tasks, not with the behavioral tasks being performed.
source: In conclusion, zona incerta activation was closely associated with movement during the tasks, not with the behavioral tasks being performed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the avoidance task data.

claim: The unsignaled US evoked a strong zona incerta activation in association with the fast escape response.
source: The unsignaled US evoked a strong zona incerta activation in association with the fast escape response.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Presentation of the foot-shock alone produced an activation and escape response that was similar to the full US.
source: Presentation of the foot-shock alone, produced an activation and escape response that was similar to the full US.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Presentation of the white noise alone drove escape responses that were somewhat slower and evoked less zona incerta activation than foot-shock alone or the full US.
source: Presentation of the white noise alone also drove escape responses, but these were somewhat slower and evoked less zona incerta activation than foot-shock alone (Tukey t(6) = 5.42, p = 0.02) or the full US (Tukey t(6) = 5.69, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The zona incerta activation during unsignaled US presentations follows the speed of the escape movement driven by the stimuli.
source: Thus, the zona incerta activation during unsignaled US presentations, follows the speed of the escape movement driven by the stimuli
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unsignaled US data.

claim: The auditory white noise component adds little to the foot-shock driven movement and its related activation.
source: and the auditory white noise component adds little to the foot-shock driven movement and its related activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the US component dissociation data.

claim: Zona incerta neurons activate to stimuli that produce movement.
source: In conclusion, zona incerta neurons activate to stimuli that produce movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various stimulation experiments.

claim: The injection of AAV8-EF1a-mCherry-flex-dtA reduced the number of zona incerta neurons.
source: The injection reduced the number of zona incerta neurons (Figure 8A, Mann–Whitney Z = 4.09, p<0.0001 Lesion vs Control).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Killing GABAergic zona incerta neurons had only minor effects on the ability of mice to learn and perform signaled active avoidance tasks.
source: However, killing GABAergic zona incerta neurons had only minor effects on the ability of mice to learn and perform signaled active avoidance tasks (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There was a small effect on the percentage of avoidance responses during the AA1 procedure in lesion mice.
source: There was a small effect on the percentage of avoidance responses during the AA1 procedure (ANOVA F(1,13) = 4.89, p = 0.043, Lesion vs Control)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There was no difference in avoidance percentage during AA2 or AA3 between lesion and control mice.
source: but not during AA2 or AA3.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There was no difference in either avoidance latency or ITCs between control and lesion mice.
source: There was no difference in either avoidance latency or ITCs between control and lesion mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The orienting response evoked by the CS onset was larger in lesion mice compared to the control mice.
source: The orienting response evoked by the CS1 onset was larger in lesion mice compared to the control mice (ANOVA F(1,343) = 64.72, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The avoidance movement speed was slower in the lesion mice compared to the control mice.
source: However, the avoidance movement speed was slower in the lesion mice compared to the control mice (ANOVA F(1,335) = 37.95, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The slower avoidance movement in lesion mice applied to both the translational and rotational movement.
source: This applied to both the translational (ANOVA F(1,335) = 44.65, p < 0.0001) and rotational (ANOVA F(1,335) = 8.44, p = 0.0039) movement.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Escape response movement was also slower in lesion mice compared to control mice.
source: Similarly, escape response movement was also slower in lesion mice compared to control mice (ANOVA F(1,250) = 8.9, p = 0.0031).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The slower escape response in lesion mice applied to translational but not rotational movement.
source: This applied to translational (ANOVA F(1,250) = 12.16, p = 0.0006) but not rotational (ANOVA F(1,250) = 1.04, p = 0.3) movement.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Lesions of GABAergic zona incerta neurons enhance the CS-evoked orienting reflex but suppress the goal-directed movement driven by the CS and US.
source: In conclusion, lesions of GABAergic zona incerta neurons enhance the CS-evoked orienting reflex but suppress the goal-directed movement driven by the CS and US.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lesion experiment data.

claim: The lesions have little impact on brain processes such as decision making (Go/NoGo in AA1–3), response inhibition (unsignaled and signaled passive avoidance in AA2/3), and stimulus discrimination (AA3).
source: The lesions have little impact on brain processes such as decision making (Go/NoGo in AA1–3), response inhibition (unsignaled and signaled passive avoidance in AA2/3), and stimulus discrimination (AA3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lesion experiment data.

claim: Application of continuous or trains of blue or green light in the zona incerta of No Opsin mice did not affect speed or head direction bias in an open field.
source: In general, application of continuous (Cont) blue or green light, or trains (1-ms pulses) of blue light at 10–20 or 40–66 Hz in the zona incerta of No Opsin mice (27 sessions in 7 mice; blue and green light are combined in Cont) while they explored an open field did not affect speed or head direction bias in an open field (Figure 9A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Unilateral inhibition of Arch-expressing GABAergic zona incerta neurons with continuous green light did not produce a significant effect on head orienting bias compared to No Opsin controls.
source: Unilateral inhibition of Arch-expressing GABAergic zona incerta neurons in Vgat-ZI-Arch mice (35 sessions in 7 mice; Figure 9A–C) with Cont green light did not produce a significant effect on head orienting bias compared to No Opsin controls (Cont vs No Opsin Tukey t(68) = 1.64404, p = 0.24915 [p = 0.218]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Inhibiting GABAergic zona incerta cells unilaterally has weak effects on head orienting movement.
source: Thus, inhibiting GABAergic zona incerta cells unilaterally has weak effects on head orienting movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unilateral inhibition data.

claim: Bilateral inhibition of zona incerta increased the overall speed of the orienting response movement.
source: Inhibiting Arch-expressing GABAergic zona incerta neurons in Vgat-ZI-Arch mice (21 sessions in 7 mice; Figure 9D) with Cont green light (during the CS–US periods) increased the overall speed of the orienting response movement (Tukey t(6) = 8.57, p = 0.0009 area; Tukey t(6) = 7.63, p = 0.0017 peak)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Bilateral inhibition of zona incerta increased the ensuing avoidance movement.
source: and increased the ensuing avoidance movement (Tukey t(6) = 5.97, p = 0.0056 area)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Bilateral inhibition of zona incerta shifted the time to peak of avoidance faster.
source: shifting the time to peak of avoidance faster (Tukey t(6) = 8.47, p = 0.001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Bilateral inhibition of zona incerta did not increase the peak avoidance speed.
source: without increasing the peak avoidance speed (Tukey t(6) = 0.01, p = 0.995).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Inhibiting zona incerta neurons enhances goal-directed movement and the orienting response driven by the CS.
source: Thus, inhibiting zona incerta neurons enhances goal-directed movement and the orienting response driven by the CS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bilateral inhibition data.

claim: Unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic zona incerta neurons with continuous and 40–66 Hz blue light evoked a contraversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls.
source: Excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic zona incerta neurons in Vgat-ZI-ChR2 mice (44 sessions in 4 mice; Figure 10A, C) with Cont and 40–66 Hz blue light evoked a contraversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls (Cont vs No Opsin Tukey t(156) = 15.48, p < 0.0001 [p < 0.0001]; 40–66 Hz vs No Opsin Tukey t(156) = 9.67, p < 0.0001 [p < 0.0001]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The strongest movement during unilateral excitation was caused by continuous blue light.
source: The strongest movement was caused by Cont blue light, which produced a sharp change in movement vigor at light onset followed by a smaller rebound at light offset.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The effect of unilateral excitation on movement vigor was virtually absent during bilateral excitation.
source: However, the effect of unilateral excitation on movement vigor was virtually absent during bilateral excitation (Figure 10B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10B-C.

claim: During exploratory behavior, unilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons evokes a vigorous contraversive movement.
source: Thus, during exploratory behavior, unilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons evokes a vigorous contraversive movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unilateral excitation data.

claim: Bilateral excitation was not associated with movement or directional bias.
source: However, bilateral excitation was not associated with movement or directional bias.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10B-C.

claim: Bilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons increased the overall speed of the orienting response movement.
source: Bilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons during performance of signaled active avoidance (AA1; Figure 10D) increased the overall (baseline subtracted) speed of the orienting response movement (Tukey t(28) = 5.64, p = 0.0004 area; Tukey t(28) = 4.19, p = 0.0062 peak)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Bilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons decreased the ensuing avoidance movement.
source: and decreased the ensuing avoidance movement (Tukey t(28) = 3.57, p = 0.0176 area; Tukey t(28) = 6.21, p = 0.0001 peak).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Exciting GABAergic zona incerta cells bilaterally suppresses avoidance movement which can impair goal-directed behavior.
source: Thus, exciting GABAergic zona incerta cells bilaterally suppresses avoidance movement which can impair goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bilateral excitation data.

claim: Unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic fibers originating in zona incerta in PO thalamus with continuous and 40–66 Hz blue light evoked a contraversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls.
source: In the PO thalamus, unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic fibers originating in zona incerta (31 sessions in 4 mice; Figure 11A, C, D) with Cont and 40–66 Hz blue light evoked a contraversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls (Cont vs No Opsin Tukey t(130) = 7.15, p < 0.0001 [p < 0.0001]; 40–66 Hz vs No Opsin Tukey t(130) = 4.16, p < 0.0001 [p < 0.0001]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 11C-D.

claim: The effects of unilateral continuous blue light in PO resemble the effects of light applied in zona incerta proper.
source: The effects of unilateral Cont blue light in PO resemble the effects of light applied in zona incerta proper.
evidence: This is a comparison of effects observed in different experiments.

claim: Continuous light applied in PO thalamus can reach the underlying zona incerta.
source: This is expected because we previously showed that Cont light applied in PO thalamus can reach the underlying zona incerta (Hormigo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: None of the effects of unilateral PO excitation were observed during bilateral excitation.
source: However, none of these effects were observed during bilateral excitation (Figure 11B–D), which is also the case when light is applied directly in zona incerta.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 11B-D.

claim: Unilateral PO inhibition caused by zona incerta firing slightly biases head orienting in the contraversive direction while bilateral PO inhibition has little effect on movement.
source: Thus, unilateral PO inhibition caused by zona incerta firing slightly biases head orienting in the contraversive direction while bilateral PO inhibition has little effect on movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PO excitation data.

claim: Unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic fibers originating in zona incerta in PPT with 40–66 Hz trains of blue light evoked a contraversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls.
source: In PPT, unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic fibers originating in zona incerta (34 sessions in 4 mice; Figure 11A, C, D) with 40–66 Hz trains of blue light, but not Cont, evoked a contraversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls (Cont vs No Opsin Tukey t(136) = 2.6, p = 0.42 [p = 0.68]; 40–66 Hz vs No Opsin Tukey t(136) = 11.23, p < 0.0001 [p < 0.0001]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 11C-D.

claim: The movement in PPT was caused selectively by trains of blue light.
source: The movement was caused selectively by trains of blue light, which produced a change in movement vigor at light onset.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The effects of movement in PPT were absent when the excitation was bilateral.
source: However, these effects of movement were absent when the excitation was bilateral (Figure 11B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 11B-D.

claim: Only unilateral PPT inhibition by zona incerta fibers biases head movement.
source: Thus, only unilateral PPT inhibition by zona incerta fibers biases head movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PPT excitation data.

claim: Unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic fibers originating in zona incerta in the superior colliculus with continuous and 40–66 Hz blue light evoked an ipsiversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls.
source: In contrast to the effects within zona incerta or projections to PO and PPT, in the superior colliculus, unilateral excitation of ChR2-expressing GABAergic fibers originating in zona incerta (23 sessions in 4 mice; Figure 11A, C, D) with Cont and 40–66 Hz blue light evoked an ipsiversive orienting head bias compared to No Opsin controls (Cont vs No Opsin Tukey t(114) = 5.58, p = 0.001 [p < 0.0001]; 40–66 Hz vs No Opsin Tukey t(114) = 3.75, p = 0.09 [p = 0.002]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 11C-D.

claim: The effects of unilateral excitation of zona incerta fibers in superior colliculus are consistent with the effects of unilateral superior colliculus inhibition with other methods.
source: The effects of unilateral excitation of zona incerta fibers in superior colliculus, which inhibits the superior colliculus, are consistent with the effects of unilateral superior colliculus inhibition with other methods (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of zona incerta GABAergic neurons has weak effects on exploratory movement.
source: In conclusion, inhibition of zona incerta GABAergic neurons has weak effects on exploratory movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic inhibition data.

claim: Unilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons produces a contraversive head orienting bias associated with a sharp increase in movement vigor at light onset that is absent during bilateral excitation.
source: In contrast, unilateral excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons produces a contraversive head orienting bias associated with a sharp increase in movement vigor at light onset that is absent during bilateral excitation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic excitation data.

claim: The unilateral effects of excitation can be mediated primarily by projections to PPT in the midbrain.
source: The unilateral effects of excitation can be mediated primarily by projections to PPT in the midbrain, but less likely by projections to PO thalamus or superior colliculus, which produce weak effects on movement or movement in the ipsiversive (opposite) direction, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the projection-specific optogenetic data.

claim: The fact that unilateral excitation of GABAergic pathways to the midbrain tegmentum and to the superior colliculus have opposite effects on movement orienting direction agrees with the finding that population activity of zona incerta GABAergic neurons measured with fiber photometry do not code orienting direction.
source: The fact that unilateral excitation of GABAergic pathways to the midbrain tegmentum and to the superior colliculus have opposite effects on movement orienting direction agrees with the finding that population activity of zona incerta GABAergic neurons measured with fiber photometry do not code orienting direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Zona incerta neurons provide a generalized movement signal to the distributed network of sites where they project.
source: We found that zona incerta neurons provide a generalized movement signal to the distributed network of sites where they project.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Electrophysiology revealed that most zona incerta neurons are modulated by movement with some neurons strongly activated and others deactivated by movement.
source: Electrophysiology revealed that most zona incerta neurons are modulated by movement with some neurons strongly activated and others deactivated by movement.
evidence: This is a summary of the electrophysiology findings.

claim: Calcium imaging showed that GABAergic zona incerta neurons activate during exploratory and goal-directed movement, but they do not code the direction of the movement.
source: Calcium imaging showed that GABAergic zona incerta neurons activate during exploratory and goal-directed movement, but they do not code the direction of the movement.
evidence: This is a summary of the calcium imaging findings.

claim: Removing (inhibiting or killing) zona incerta GABAergic neurons had little impact on behavioral performance.
source: Although zona incerta GABAergic neurons activate during goal-directed behaviors, removing (inhibiting or killing) these neurons had little impact on behavioral performance.
evidence: This is a summary of the lesion and inhibition findings.

claim: Removing zona incerta neurons modulated movement parameters, such as goal-directed speed and CS-evoked orienting responses.
source: Removing these neurons modulated movement parameters, such as goal-directed speed and CS-evoked orienting responses, which highlights a role of zona incerta in sensorimotor regulation, but animals performed the tasks at control levels.
evidence: This is a summary of the lesion and inhibition findings.

claim: Optogenetic excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons can suppress goal-directed movement and impact behavioral performance.
source: Although optogenetic excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons can suppress goal-directed movement and impact behavioral performance (Hormigo et al., 2020), this may represent an abnormal level of activation associated with pathological states.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and interpretation of the current findings.

claim: The levels of optogenetic excitation that suppress behavioral performance are likely distinct from the levels of activation associated with normal movement.
source: Furthermore, when we recorded from these neurons, we found a robust activation during goal-directed movement, which emphasizes the point that the levels of optogenetic excitation that suppress behavioral performance are likely distinct from the levels of activation associated with normal movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined findings.

claim: The role of zona incerta activation cannot be to drive the behavior but to inform its targets that the behavior is occurring, which can be used to modulate the behavior.
source: Since the removal of this activation has little impact on behavioral performance, the role of zona incerta activation cannot be to drive the behavior but to inform its targets that the behavior is occurring, which can be used to modulate the behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined findings.

claim: Auditory inputs are located laterally in zona incerta in rats.
source: Consistent with the existence of auditory inputs located laterally and somatosensory inputs distributed throughout zona incerta in rats (Mitrofanis, 2002; Shaw and Mitrofanis, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Somatosensory inputs are distributed throughout zona incerta in rats.
source: Consistent with the existence of auditory inputs located laterally and somatosensory inputs distributed throughout zona incerta in rats (Mitrofanis, 2002; Shaw and Mitrofanis, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies have shown that zona incerta neurons discharge in response to auditory and whisker stimulation under various conditions.
source: previous studies have shown that zona incerta neurons discharge in response to auditory and whisker stimulation under various conditions (Trageser et al., 2006; Urbain and Deschênes, 2007; Wang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A sensory integrative function has been proposed as the main role of zona incerta.
source: Thus, a sensory integrative function has been proposed as its main role (Mitrofanis, 2005; Wang et al., 2020a; Fratzl and Hofer, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During auditory mapping sessions, zona incerta GABAergic neurons discharged in response to auditory stimuli that did not predict any behavioral contingencies.
source: We found that during auditory mapping sessions, zona incerta GABAergic neurons discharged in response to auditory stimuli that did not predict any behavioral contingencies.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The auditory stimuli that activated zona incerta neurons were invariably associated with movement.
source: However, the auditory stimuli that activated zona incerta neurons were invariably associated with movement.
evidence: This is an observation from the auditory mapping data.

claim: Light isoflurane anesthesia was required to abolish the evoked movements, which also strongly suppressed or abolished the sensory-evoked responses in zona incerta.
source: Light isoflurane anesthesia was required to abolish the evoked movements, which also strongly suppressed or abolished the sensory-evoked responses in zona incerta.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Zona incerta GABAergic neurons respond to salient auditory stimuli primarily in association with movement.
source: Taken together, the results indicate that zona incerta GABAergic neurons respond to salient auditory stimuli primarily in association with movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the auditory stimulation experiments.

claim: The orienting reflex is a basic sensorimotor behavior that consists of a fast (<300 ms) head movement in association with presentation of sensory stimuli.
source: The orienting reflex is a basic sensorimotor behavior that consists of a fast (<300 ms) head movement in association with presentation of sensory stimuli (Sokolov, 1963), which is modulated by behavioral states (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lesions of zona incerta GABAergic neurons produced a large increase of the orienting response evoked by the CS in the context of signaled goal-directed avoidance behavior.
source: Intriguingly, lesions of zona incerta GABAergic neurons produced a large increase of the orienting response evoked by the CS in the context of signaled goal-directed avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The enhanced orienting reflex in lesion animals contrasted with the suppression of the goal-directed movement in the same lesion animals.
source: Moreover, the enhanced orienting reflex contrasted with the suppression of the goal-directed movement in the same lesion animals.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition or excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons augmented the CS-evoked orienting responses.
source: Similarly, optogenetic inhibition or excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons augmented the CS-evoked orienting responses in the same context.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 9-10.

claim: The zona incerta has access to areas that control the orienting reflex.
source: Thus, the zona incerta has access to areas that control the orienting reflex.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed effects on orienting.

claim: Zona incerta projections to midbrain areas, such as the superior colliculus, can mediate effects on the orienting reflex.
source: Indeed, zona incerta projections to midbrain areas, such as the superior colliculus (Zhou et al., 2023), can easily mediate these effects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and the current findings.

claim: The brainstem nuclei responsible for the orienting reflex may be under tonic zona incerta inhibitory control.
source: One possibility is that the brainstem nuclei responsible for the orienting reflex are under tonic zona incerta inhibitory control and removing or dampening this inhibition augments the orienting reflex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Zona incerta must be considered as part of the circuitry that may control the orienting response during different behavioral states.
source: Since zona incerta can modulate the orienting reflex, it must be considered as part of the circuitry that may control this response during different behavioral states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the orienting reflex findings.

claim: In head-fixed mice on the spherical treadmill, zona incerta neurons discharge in relation to the occurrence of movement.
source: In head-fixed mice on the spherical treadmill, we found that zona incerta neurons discharge in relation to the occurrence of movement.
evidence: This is a summary of the electrophysiology findings.

claim: Most of the tested units did not respond to auditory stimuli perhaps because unit sampling missed the lateral parts of zona incerta.
source: Most of the tested units did not respond to auditory stimuli perhaps because our unit sampling missed the lateral parts of zona incerta, which receive auditory input in rats (Mitrofanis, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: A small percentage of neurons responded to whisker stimulation, but these neurons belonged to both Class1 and Class2.
source: A small percentage of neurons responded to whisker stimulation, but these neurons belonged to both Class1 and Class2, indicating that they were not associated with a particular sensitivity to movement.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fiber photometry calcium imaging of zona incerta GABAergic neurons revealed a robust zona incerta neuron activation during exploratory movement.
source: In agreement with the unit data, fiber photometry calcium imaging of zona incerta GABAergic neurons revealed a robust zona incerta neuron activation during exploratory movement.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The robust activation of zona incerta neurons did not code the orienting direction of the exploratory movement.
source: However, the robust activation of these neurons did not code the orienting direction of the exploratory movement.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Zona incerta neurons discharge during movement occurrence regardless of the animal's turning direction.
source: Zona incerta neurons discharge during movement occurrence regardless of the animal's turning direction, which contrasts with one of its targets, the superior colliculus, that clearly codes the orienting direction using the same recording methods (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citation to previous work.

claim: Zona incerta neurons were strongly activated during avoidance and escape movements.
source: Zona incerta neurons were strongly activated during avoidance and escape movements.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: Passive avoids driven by auditory stimuli, which are not associated with movement, did not activate zona incerta neurons.
source: Passive avoids driven by auditory stimuli, which are not associated with movement, did not activate zona incerta neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Zona incerta does not cause the suppression of movement associated with passive avoids because there was little activation of these neurons during signaled passive avoidance trials.
source: Moreover, although excitation of zona incerta GABAergic neurons can suppress active avoids, zona incerta does not cause the suppression of movement associated with passive avoids because there was little activation of these neurons during signaled passive avoidance trials (CS2 in AA3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the passive avoidance data.

claim: Lesions or optogenetic inhibition of zona incerta GABAergic neurons affected movement speed during the goal-directed behaviors but had little impact on the ability of mice to successfully perform the tasks.
source: Lesions or optogenetic inhibition of zona incerta GABAergic neurons affected movement speed during the goal-directed behaviors but had little impact on the ability of mice to successfully perform the tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the lesion and inhibition findings.

claim: The regulation of speed by zona incerta was bidirectional; excitation of zona incerta suppresses goal-directed movement while inhibition of zona incerta facilitates goal-directed movement.
source: Moreover, this regulation of speed was bidirectional; excitation of zona incerta suppresses goal-directed movement while inhibition of zona incerta facilitates goal-directed movement.
evidence: This is a summary of the optogenetic manipulation findings.

claim: If zona incerta activation is strong it would inhibit the brainstem targets that generate the ongoing movement to keep it under control.
source: For instance, if zona incerta activation is strong it would inhibit the brainstem targets that generate the ongoing movement to keep it under control (within certain parameters), as part of a regulatory control system (Sommer and Wurtz, 2008; Yin, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The zona incerta would function as a sensor of ongoing movement that feeds control circuits in the brainstem through its projections to keep the behavior within certain parameters defined by the situation.
source: Thus, the zona incerta would function as a sensor of ongoing movement that feeds control circuits in the brainstem through its projections to keep the behavior within certain parameters defined by the situation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: An important role of zona incerta neurons is to signal to target structures that movement is occurring, which is useful to regulate ongoing behavior.
source: We conclude that an important role of zona incerta neurons is to signal to target structures that movement is occurring, which is useful to regulate ongoing behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
